extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, astronomers, and mathematicians (readers/contributors to Philosophical Transactions / Royal Society)
extracted.subtask_description: Composing and reporting observational accounts, theoretical treatises, and methodological proposals for natural philosophy, astronomy, and mathematics as presented in a 17th-century scientific journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and growth of hair
rubrics_metrics.description: The skin of the hair is made up of globules forming a bark; the innermost parts of the hair are made up of threads; hair grows not like plants but by protrusion or squeezing outwards from within the skin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When first protruded the hair is soft and then dries in the air, first drying in the bark so that inward parts shrink and cleave, producing inward clefts that sometimes appear hollow and are mistaken for marrow. Drawings (e.g. of a hog's bristle) help to show that apparent hollowness is the inward clefts rather than true marrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic examination of fresh excrements and urine
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine fresh excrements and thick parts of urine microscopically; many small globules may be found in clear liquor, varying in size relative to a blood globule (e.g. 1/6, 1/36, 1/8 etc.), and compound globules composed of several smaller globules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect fresh material (meadows' excrements, squeezed dung, urine of a mare after hard riding). Squeeze out fresh dung to look for worms (example: in cock's dung found many worms like eels identified as male seed), press young pigeons' dung to find moving egg-shaped bodies. Note sizes by comparison to a blood globule and record composition (some globules composed of 3–6 others). Use immediate examination after excretion to avoid later changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comet interpretation principles (Fontaney's conclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret comet observations using the following principles: (1) the blaze/tail is caused by the rays of the sun passing through the head; (2) these rays are received/reflected by matter denser than the aether; (3) the head is not made up of small fixed stars (not a stellar nebula); (4) the head must both transmit and reflect rays and can differ in density from the blaze; (5) the head is usually more dense than the blaze but need not be round; (6) transparency alone is not enough — the head must give greater power to rays projected to enlighten parts behind it; (7) convex parts in the head form conic unions of rays creating brighter parts of the blaze; (8) a comet can be formed by unions of denser convex parts of nebulous matter disposed into convenient order, analogous to atmospheric mock-suns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use telescopic appearance (e.g. head seen as dusky light differing from stars/planets, sometimes multiple nuclei that divide/unite) and tail geometry relative to sun to infer density, transparency, and structure. Consider comet as a 'celestial meteor' whose optical effects follow from arrangement of condensed parts; compare to parhelia (mock suns) as an explanatory analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: comets generated de novo in lower regions (Rossetti)
rubrics_metrics.description: A theoretical stance that comets may be generated de novo and dispersed in the elementary regions about the earth rather than existing only in very high regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing comet distance/placement, take into account that refraction of rays through the atmosphere may cause large irregularities; arguments from little or no parallax are not necessarily decisive because atmospheric refraction can perturb apparent positions and prevent sufficiently exact tables for planets or comets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions used for predicting comet motion (Anthelme/Dijon tract)
rubrics_metrics.description: To predict a comet's appearance and motion one may assume: comets are bodies as old as creation; they move with regular motions comparable to planets in very eccentric orbs; their bodies are transparent transmitting the sun's beams (making the tail opposite the sun); and comets have no necessary significance for terrestrial events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictions (tables of appearance/disappearance and daily motion in longitude/latitude) built from early observations rely on these assumptions about orbital regularity and transparency. Be explicit about hypotheses used, as different hypotheses yield different predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining longitude from lunar occultations (Halley's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find longitude differences by observing lunar occultations (applications of the Moon to a star) at different locations, recording precise immersion and emersion times, and comparing these to determine the Moon's place at corresponding times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a pendulum watch rectified by solar altitudes and rising/setting times to time events accurately at each station; compute the Moon's true place corrected for parallax; use the Moon's known velocity to convert angular differences between observed places into time differences, yielding difference of longitude. Cross-validate with independent observers (e.g. Flamsteed, Hevelius) and multiple events to confirm results. Record observational circumstances (latitude, local time when equal altitudes occurred, instrument details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Monitor — three core organizing questions (Pell)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Mathematical Monitor' should contain answers to three questions: 1) What advantages may be expected from the study of the mathematics? 2) What helps are now extant for attaining that knowledge? 3) What order is to be employed in using those helps?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three questions as the organizing principle for any comprehensive guide to the mathematical sciences, ensuring the Monitor addresses expected benefits, available resources, and recommended pedagogy/sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Monitor — discourse on limits and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a clear and easy discourse on the limits or extent of the mathematical arts and of the benefits that may accrue, both to students and to the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain practical and theoretical advantages, national utility, and personal benefits; present in accessible language to persuade patrons and students of the value of mathematical study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue of mathematicians and their works (Monitor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide (1) a synopsis of all kinds of mathematical books (print and MS) with reference numbers; (2) a chronological catalogue of celebrated mathematicians with dates of their works; (3) a catalogue of works ordered by year of printing in any language, noting form and quantity of each volume and cross-referencing to the synopsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange catalogues to enable easy reference: place the year before the title and the most recent reprint year after; include numbers referring back to the synopsis page. The catalogue should indicate where copies can be had and reduce search time for scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice to students on selection, order, and retention of books
rubrics_metrics.description: Give explicit advice concerning the best books of every kind, in what order and method to read them, which parts to select or omit, and how to retain material in memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide study plans, methods for selecting essential passages, mnemonic/memory techniques, and guidance to avoid spending time on matter already treated; help students prioritize and retain crucial concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhortation to patrons and encouragement mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Urge persons of wealth, leisure, and genius to pursue mathematical studies and encourage patrons to offer handsome rewards to support completion of useful discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for public and private patronage as part of advancing science; recommend showing the value of mathematics to princes and the public to secure endowments and support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public library and librarian duties for mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a public library furnished with all relevant mathematical books and at least one instrument of every kind, endowed for purchases and for a librarian. The librarian's duties include reading over books published in the country, suppressing useless or erroneous works, admonishing authors who publish only known things, recommending inventors to patrons, receiving and cataloguing presented books and manuscripts, advising students, keeping correspondence with learned foreigners, and evaluating practical instrument-makers and operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the library as a national resource: maintain copies of all mathematical works, receive one bound copy of works presented by authors/booksellers, offer civil and ready answers to queries to avoid duplication of effort, keep records of leading practitioners, and after fair trials give testimony on both speculative knowledge and practical dexterity so users are not imposed upon by pretenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Pandects (encyclopedic collected corollaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose 'Mathematical Pandects' containing, methodically and concisely, all that may be collected or deduced as corollaries from previous mathematical works, citing the most ancient authors and indicating where later authors have appropriated others' results without acknowledgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pandects to compress the large extant library into a narrower, authoritative compendium to save labor, time, and expense for future scholars; include clear chains of reasoning from first principles to highest applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Compendium (concise manual and tables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce a concise compendium containing the most useful tables and precepts showing their application to solving problems of pure mathematics and applied subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the compendium a practical quick-reference manual that facilitates computation and application across disciplines; include example precepts for applying tables to problem-solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficient Mathematician (instruction for independent problem-solving)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide instruction enabling a mathematician, by industry and without aversion to labour, to acquire skill sufficient to solve any mathematical problem without the aid of books or instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach methods for strengthening imagination, assisting memory, and directing reasoning; aim to fix key processes so firmly that reliance on books/instruments is reduced or unnecessary for routine problem-solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of authors and condensation over exhaustive collection (Mersenne)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer selecting only the best and most deserving authors in each area rather than assembling every existing work and apparatus; choose a small number of exemplars per subfield to be abridged into concise volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with ancient authors still extant (Euclid, Apollonius, Archimedes, etc.), then add the best moderns for each subfield. A small committee (e.g. 12 men) could produce 12 clear volumes to cover mathematics; choose 8–12 key authors for mechanics/waterworks, and a few for other applied areas. This approach favors curation and quality over quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument selection principle
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient to procure four or five of the best instruments of each kind rather than an apparatus consisting of every instrument ever invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the most convenient and useful instruments; prioritize quality and representativeness rather than completeness when equipping a public mathematical collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression of knowledge into limited representative volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose compressing mathematics into a manageable set (e.g. 12 volumes for mathematics, 3 for neat parts of philosophy, 3 for liberal/mechanic arts) by having experts abridge essential works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to supply comprehensive learning in a small, accessible set of authoritative volumes prepared by selected skilled authors, thereby reducing expense and accelerating learning.
